USA.rationale:
RECOMMENDATION: Hold the current posture and press the Phase One agreement to a signed, enforceable conclusion without imposing new tariffs. In particular, do not pull the trigger on the pending December 15 consumer-goods tariff (phones, laptops, toys), which would fall on US-designed products, consumers and markets and could collapse the fragile truce — but do not unilaterally roll back existing tariffs either until China's agricultural-purchase and IP commitments are actually delivered and enforceable. Keep negotiating with China pushing for rollbacks; our leverage is strongest now, before signature.

SUPPORTING RATIONALE: Threat is moderate, not existential. The US has extracted real concessions — China committing to ~$40-50B of annual agricultural purchases, plus IP and financial/currency steps (timeline 2019-10-11; Politico/Livemint). The economy shows strain but resilience: the Fed cut funds from 2.38% to 1.55% amid slowing industrial production and a 10-yr at 1.73%, yet consumer sentiment recovered to 96.8 and Baa spreads narrowed (country_health). The residual risk is a deal collapse and the Dec 15 consumer-goods tariff, which would hit US-designed products, markets, and could invite Chinese retaliation — a real but manageable ~+0.2 threat. This justifies a hold/negotiate stance rather than escalation: escalation via the Dec 15 round would be largely self-inflicted and risks destroying the most favourable negotiation terrain the US has had all year, while full concession would forfeit leverage before China has performed. So an action_score near zero with negotiate is the disciplined read — hold the cards, finish the deal, and decide any rollback only in exchange for verified delivery.

CHN.rationale:
RECOMMENDATION: Hold the current negotiating posture and push to finalize and sign the Phase One deal, which offers a concrete path to freezing further tariff escalation and beginning a phased rollback. We should not escalate — the domestic economy is already feeling real pain and new tariffs would deepen the downturn — but we should also not concede beyond the agricultural-purchase commitments already announced. Lock in the agreement while preserving our demand for phased tariff removal and Huawei relief in later phases.

SUPPORTING RATIONALE: The threat is high but not existential, so I read it at +0.4. The export economy is demonstrably under pressure: industrial production rose only 4.7% in October versus a 5.4% forecast, manufacturing has been in contraction for six straight months, GDP growth of 6.0% is near a 30-year low, and exports have fallen for three consecutive months (Oct -0.9%) — all against a backdrop of tariffs on virtually our entire export basket (List 3 at 25%, List 4 at 15%, with ~$160B more scheduled for Dec 15) and Huawei on the Entity List (timeline, May 16; country_health; Guardian/CNBC, Nov 14). Mitigating that reading to below the +0.5-%2B.7 existential band are the stability anchors: FX reserves held steady near US$3.1T, the RMB stabilized around 7.0 after recovering from the 7.15 August low, and the discount rate (2.9%) is untouched, leaving real stimulus headroom. The action stance is mildly conciliatory (+0.15 / negotiate) because the de-escalation track is real and already in motion: the Phase One deal in principle (Oct 11) commits us to $40-50B of US farm purchases in exchange for suspending escalation, and both sides reportedly agreed on Nov 8 to phased tariff rollbacks. Given the economy's genuine strain, the rational move is to secure that deal rather than risk a breakdown that would trigger the Dec 15 tariff and deepen the slowdown. This is engagement with limited new commitments, not capitulation: we keep the phased-rollback and Huawei issues on the table for subsequent phases.
